description: Lunar Silk Road is a free mission trainer where students keep a crew of four alive on the Moon or Mars, balancing power, life support, food and radiation shielding in a live 3D base. At its heart is silk: mulberry, silkworms, silk and protein in a closed loop taken from real life-support research. We love space science, education and the idea that one of humanity's oldest materials could help us live beyond Earth. Challenge: Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer.
summary:
Lunar Silk Road is a free browser game that trains junior astronauts to run a base on the Moon or Mars. Each turn is one week. Students decide where the power goes, what to build and when to shield the crew. Then the week plays out, with two-week lunar nights, solar storms and, on Mars, dust storms that hide the Sun for weeks.

What holds the base together is silk. Based on published life-support research, mulberry plants make oxygen and leaves, silkworms turn the leaves into silk and protein, and their droppings fertilize the crops. Silk becomes clothes, sutures, building material, trade goods and finally a dome woven over the whole base.

The game answers the challenge directly: life support, radiation, power and food all pull against each other, and every mission ends with a debrief that explains what decided it. A Design Lab lets students test a base for a whole year. Every number has a source or is labelled as our own assumption.

It matters because a base far from Earth must grow what it needs. Lunar Silk Road shows students that one of humanity's oldest materials could help us live beyond Earth. It works offline, and the website is in six languages.
details:
What it does

Students aged about 10 to 15 pick one of three missions:

- Training Base (Moon, 12 weeks): a step-by-step coach.

- Artemis Moon Base (16 weeks): 14-day nights, solar storms, Silk Road trade with Earth.

- Mars Pioneer (20 weeks): weaker sunlight, no resupply ships, a 2018-style global dust storm, and MOXIE-style oxygen from CO₂.

Each week the crew has two actions. They can build modules with a limited number of kits (solar panels, batteries, crop farms, mulberry groves, silkworm rooms), operate the base (pile regolith shielding, clean dusty panels, rest), or use their silk.

How it works

- Power: panels produce only in sunlight. When power runs short, modules shut down in a fixed order (silkworm rooms, then mulberry groves, then farms, with life support last), so trade-offs are visible.

- Silkworm life cycle: each room shows its stage: hatching, 4th instar, 5th instar (when a silkworm eats about 80% of all the leaves it will eat) and cocoon spinning. After 4 weeks a room yields silk, 3 weeks of protein and fertilizer (+30% crops). One bad week pauses growth; two in a row lose the batch. Pebrine disease can strike.

- Radiation: a weekly cosmic-ray dose based on the lunar-surface rate measured by Chang'e 4, plus solar particle events. Regolith shielding and stacked food and water reduce the dose. Engineer View shows the total in mSv and as a percentage of NASA's 600 mSv career limit.

- Great Silk Dome: a megastructure built in three stages (frame and tethers, woven restraint layer, seal and inflate). Once complete, it adds food and oxygen in sunlight without grow lights.

- Debrief: lessons are generated from what actually happened. Charts mark nights, storms and blackouts. There are three discussion questions, a copyable mission report, and a "replay same mission" option.

Learn, design, scale

- CAPCOM advisor and Undo: beginners get a suggested move with a reason (press A), and any action can be taken back within the week (press U).

- Design Lab: the same model runs 52 weeks instantly without random events. An optimizer tests 4,635 designs in about 50 ms. For example, the lightest Moon base with no blackouts and at least 80% of food and protein made on site needs 13 build kits.

- Scale-up calculator: uses 20–25 g of leaves per silkworm (Japan MLIT guide), 0.21–0.31 g and 941–994 m of filament per cocoon (Rathod et al., 2015) and 30–35 t/ha/yr irrigated mulberry yields (FAO). At 2 kg of raw silk per person per year, 100 people would need about 770,000 silkworms and 17 t of leaves a year, and the joined cocoon threads would stretch about twice the Earth–Moon distance.

- Model & Methods: weekly mass and energy balance equations, a parameter table rated A (measured or official) / B (rounded from published data) / C (game assumption), validation checks (for example, the game's cosmic-ray dose matches the Chang'e 4 measurement of 1.369 mSv/day), stated limitations, and a CSV export of every mission for data analysis.

- Teacher guide: a 45-minute lesson plan, learning objectives, links to NGSS MS-ETS1-1 to 4 and MS-LS2-3 and to the Japanese lower-secondary science and technology curriculum, plus a 5-question check.

Benefits and intended impact

Silk is the thread that ties the project together. People have raised silkworms for thousands of years, silk gave its name to the Silk Road between China and Europe, and Japan's Tomioka Silk Mill (1872, UNESCO World Heritage since 2014) helped turn it into a modern industry. Lunar Silk Road asks whether this ancient material could help people live beyond Earth, and uses that question to engage students in science.

Students feel engineering trade-offs before they read about them. They practise systems thinking: power, plants, insects, crew health and radiation are linked, and fixing one part can break another. Teachers get a no-install classroom tool with identical missions for fair comparison. The ideas carry over to life on Earth in deserts, polar stations and disaster zones.

Deliverables

A project website with the trailer, challenge alignment and science; the game (play.html); a 6-page technical report (model, parameter ratings, validation, strategy experiments, design optimization, sensitivity analysis, scale-up, curriculum alignment, limitations); and a 30-second trailer.

Tools

An installable, offline-capable web app (PWA) with no build step. The live 3D outpost uses Three.js (bundled, MIT). It has crater terrain, sun-tracking solar panels, walking astronauts, a Silk Road rocket launch, Mars dust-storm particles and bloom lighting. A 2D mode is included for older devices. Sound and ambient music come from a small WebAudio synthesizer. Missions use a seeded random generator, named mulberry32, which suits a silkworm game. The balance was tested automatically with Playwright bots across all three missions and several seeds: good play earns Gold or Silver, while doing nothing fails on Mars.

Creativity

Most base-building games treat food as one number. We started from a question instead: silk grows from leaves and sunlight, while synthetic fibers need oil and factories, so what could silk farming do for people living off Earth? That led us to a real life-support design that already includes silkworms. In the game, one small animal connects oxygen, food, clothing, medicine, morale, trade and, eventually, a structure too big to launch from Earth.

Factors we considered

- Age-appropriate failure: the crew "returns to Earth early" and nobody dies.

- Clear units: game units are explained, and Engineer View gives real-world equivalents.

- Accessibility: keyboard shortcuts, reduced-motion support, and text labels next to every icon.

- Honesty about the science: silk is weaker than Vectran, the fabric used in today's inflatable habitats. The silk trade and the Great Silk Dome are labelled as future concepts, not existing technology.
